title: For Maple the Pool and Token addresses are identical, while Aave keeps Pool as a separate parameter still left unspecified
content:
The Maple USDC instance lists Token Address `0x80ac24aA929eaF5013f6436cdA2a7ba190f5Cc0b` (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.3.1.2.2.1) and then `Pool` with the **same** address (.3.1.2.2.3). Maple USDT repeats the pattern: token and pool both `0x356B8d89c1e1239Cbbb9dE4815c39A1474d5BA7D` (.3.2.2.2.1, .3.2.2.2.3).

In the Aave instances the `Pool` slot exists but is empty — "This parameter will be specified in a future iteration of the Spark Artifact" (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.2.1.2.2.3).

The divergence reflects the two protocol shapes. Maple's syrup tokens are vault shares whose contract *is* the pool, so the two fields necessarily coincide and the `Pool` entry is redundant. Aave separates the aToken from the lending pool, so the pool is a genuinely distinct address — and, as the Aave process definitions show, one that is retrievable at runtime via `IAavePool(IATokenWithPool(aToken).POOL())`.

That runtime retrievability is likely why deferring Aave's `Pool` is tolerable where deferring a signer set is not: the value is derivable from a documented address, so the omission costs convenience rather than verifiability. It also shows the template carrying a slot that is meaningless for one protocol family and redundant for another — the price of a uniform schema across heterogeneous venues.
description: syrupUSDC and syrupUSDT are their own pools, so the vault token IS the venue; Aave's Pool is a distinct contract retrievable from the aToken, which is why the Artifact can defer it.
